newsitem.title: USA: Alaska lawmakers approve big tobacco tax hike.
newsitem.headline: Alaska lawmakers approve big tobacco tax hike.

text.p: Starting in October, Alaska will have the nation's highest tobacco tax, thanks to a measure passed over the weekend by the state legislature.

By a slight margin, the Republican-controlled House of Representatives approved a bill that hikes state taxes by 71 cents per pack on cigarettes and a like amount on other tobacco products. That will add to the state's current tax of 29 cents a pack.
The House action followed earlier approval by the state Senate. On Sunday, the Senate consented to minor changes in the bill, sending it to Gov. Tony Knowles for his signature and enactment into law.

Two Republican lawmakers and Knowles, a Democrat, had each sponsored bills seeking to raise the tax by $1. The 71-cent compromise, struck to gain additional votes, was acceptable but less desirable than the original proposal, said Knowles, a longtime anti-smoking activist.
Alaska's debate has been part of a national campaign to raise tobacco taxes and discourage cash-strapped youths from starting the tobacco habit.
"Alaska is in the lead, and with this I can assure you the whole world is watching," Knowles said of the legislature's action.

Proponents argue that because nearly all smokers and tobacco chewers begin their addiction by the time they are 19, a stiff tax will eventually diminish overall smoking. It will also help raise money to offset tobacco-related public health costs, they say.

Alaska has one of the highest smoking rates in the nation, and had the highest rate of smokeless tobacco use among young people. Tobacco use is heaviest among Alaska Natives in the state's far-flung rural villages; at least four out of 10 Alaska Eskimos, Indians and Aleuts smoke, according to state figures.
The state's geographical isolation makes the prospect of cigarette smuggling unlikely, proponents say.
And it needed a new revenue source to replace dwindling oil receipts. Alaska imposes few taxes on its citizens, thanks to its oil wealth. There is no personal income tax and no state sales tax.
Opponents -- almost all Republicans -- cited philosophical objections to taxing.
State Rep. Ramona Barnes, a heavy smoker, vowed to skirt the tax.

"I'm not going to pay it, plain and simple. I'm going to import cigarettes, a case at a time, 48 cartons in a case, stick them in my freezer. They'll stay just as fresh as can be. And when I want a new carton, I'll simply walk down to the freezer, take it out and pay less than I pay today," Barnes said in debate on the measure.
Opponents also tried unsuccessfully to exempt cigars and pipe tobacco.
"It is a special consumption pattern used by middle-aged, old men," said State Rep. Al Vezey.

Added State Rep. Pete Kott, who likes to lounge around the capitol with an unsmoked cigar clenched between his teeth: "George Burns lived to be a ripe old age. He smoked a couple of cigars on a daily basis."

In addition, the House raised the legal age for tobacco use to 21 from 19. It stiffened the penalties for underage purchases of cigarettes or other tobacco products, passing a bill that mandates a $250 fine for the first offense. And it outlawed self-service tobacco displays, requiring all sales to be conducted in person.
Those provisions must be passed by the Senate to become law.
Young smokers in downtown Juneau greeted the new bills with dismay.

"It's no fair to me, because I make very little money and I'm addicted to nicotine," said Will Childress, 24, a fast-food worker taking a cigarette break. "What are they going to do with the money, give themselves a raise?"
"If you're over 18 you can fight for your country. You pay taxes. You're able to vote. Why can't we smoke?" said a 16-year-old girl, identifying herself only as Donna, as she drew on a cigarette.
